airbrakes: The competition rewards hitting the apogee you declare before launch. In 2023, without active control, the team came within 1,500 ft of its 30,000 ft target: 4th closest of 32 teams and best in the hybrid and liquid category. For 2024 the team added airbrakes to steer the rocket onto its target in flight. I worked across the whole subsystem: mechanical, simulation and firmware.
After researching other teams' designs and talking with mechanical engineering professors at Waterloo, I set four requirements:
One relatively low-power servo drives everything
All three panels extend together and are always in sync
Panel extension is linear in servo rotation
As compact and light as possible

A cam-and-slot mechanism met the first two, but a standard slot isn't linear. I modified the slot profile so extension is proportional to rotation, put three of these spirals on one spinning plate, one per panel, and designed the rest of the assembly around it. I did the mechanical design independently.

With a teammate I ran Ansys CFD on the panels to check that deploying them keeps the centre of pressure safely behind the centre of gravity, and to map drag coefficient against extension for the trajectory model.

With about ten others on the subteam I wrote embedded C on an STM32 under FreeRTOS: state estimation, fourth-order Runge-Kutta apogee prediction, and closed-loop control of panel extension to hit the target apogee.
The rocket flew, but the propellant was underfilled by more than the airbrakes could correct for, so they correctly stayed retracted the whole flight.

For 2025 the team moved to roll-control canards, and I designed the new 4-layer central avionics board in KiCad. It raised power efficiency from 66% to 95%, with an onboard IMU over I²C, an external AHRS over UART and a second external IMU over I²C.
fyelabs: Industrial garbage trucks reversing in harsh, dirty conditions need to reliably avoid people and objects. The sensing unit on the back of the truck carries 10 LiDARs, 3 depth cameras, an infrared camera, a light sensor, an IMU and GPS, run by 3 microcontrollers and 4 mini compute units, all in a weatherproof housing that protects the sensors when the truck isn't reversing.

I designed the all-metal, actuating enclosure: over 100 parts across 15 major revisions covering electronics, sensor placement and manufacturability. Redesigning most of the structure as 6 sheet-metal parts, cut, bent and welded, instead of CNC milling cut manufacturing cost by 56% and halved lead time. My gasket and geometry design kept the electronics dry in a water-spray test.

The dashboard HMI is the driver's link to the unit on the back of the truck. I did all of it: the plastic case, a custom 2-layer PCB with two microcontrollers (one for the wireless link; one for 4 buttons, a speaker and a 7" display), and the firmware for both. After testing several wireless options I built a custom LoRa protocol with checksums for reliable data across 6 microcontrollers, plus a 12-zone mapping that shows the driver where a detected object is.

The LiDAR array is 10 single-beam sensors in an arc, which is robust with no moving parts but too sparse for standard point-cloud filtering, and dust was causing false positives. I collected distance and return-intensity data in clean and dusty conditions; from it, my supervisors and I developed five filters that run in parallel to ignore dust and still catch a person. I implemented them in C++ firmware on the LiDAR board.

To tune the filters I wrote a Python LiDAR visualiser: first a serial interceptor, then a wireless MQTT version so the unit could be fully sealed during tests, with recording to a custom file format and real-time playback. It let the whole team help tune the filter constants.
magna: A real-time integrity monitor for an industrial hydraulic press, using strain gauges embedded near the die. I built the pipeline end to end: sensor data streamed over MQTT, re-synchronized and stored in PostgreSQL, plus a web dashboard where operators and engineers compare strain profiles across batches and review anomalies.

I designed an anomaly detection algorithm that finds the characteristic discontinuity in the strain signatures across four sensors when a part cracks during forming. Running in real time, it caught every cracked part with zero false positives over a 150-part validation run, removing defective parts from the line automatically. It recognizes when a different part is being stamped, and a moving-window average stops slow sensor drift from being flagged.

The press's PLC had very little memory. A patent-pending buffering system I engineered, with semaphore-driven multithreading and staged data queues, let it stream far more data, raising collection from about 140 Hz to over 500 Hz for much finer analysis of each stroke.
ixana: A high-bandwidth video stream from smart glasses to a smartwatch over Ixana's YR22 silicon. It uses electro-quasistatic body communication, turning the wearer's body into a secure, ultra-low-power data bus that uses less power than Bluetooth or Wi-Fi.
I worked across the whole stack, from capture on the glasses through compression, transmission and decompression to the watch display, and was primarily responsible for the watch display drivers.
Bare metal: a power-efficient core OS in C++ for Ambiq and NXP ARM MCUs, scheduling real-time video tasks
System bring-up: debugged and helped build the full path, from camera to encoding FPGA, transmitter MCU, Wi-R silicon, receiver MCU and decoding FPGA to the AMOLED display
Signal integrity: resolved timing and data-encoding issues at the display interface
measurement: A station for quality assurance on an automation line that checks part tolerances right after manufacturing with no human involved. A part goes on a rotary platform; computer vision turns it to the orientation of its critical dimension; a clamp on a rotary encoder closes on it and stops on firm contact using force sensing, and the encoder rotation becomes a length. Out-of-spec parts have their image and failing dimension logged to a remote server, with a notice on the machine's display.

I was the lead firmware engineer: C++ on the ESP32 and the main controller for all motor control, dimension derivation and the GUI. I also worked with a teammate on the OpenCV orientation detection in Python, which sends the angle to the ESP32 over WebSockets.

The VEX V5 brain runs proprietary firmware with no UART, I²C or SPI, only the ability to read a pin as high or low. So the ESP32 receives the angle wirelessly from the PC and sends it to the brain over two wires using a protocol we designed, loosely inspired by I²C, with a clock line and a data line. The brain decodes the binary angle into encoder ticks and turns the part to the right orientation.
platform: The course platform balances a 2.7 g ping-pong ball under an overhead camera. Our team of five set out to find the ball by feel instead: a ForceN 3-axis force-torque sensor under the plate reads the normal force and the two tipping moments, and the ball's position follows from them. A ping-pong ball barely registers on a load cell, so we switched to a 538 g, 2-inch 440C steel ball, 200 times heavier. That one change broke almost every part of the platform, and redesigning the mechanics around it was my main job.
A plate that is stiff and light

Any flex in the plate corrupts the moments the sensor reads, yet every gram it adds loads the links and servos. My first plate, three 3 mm laser-cut acrylic discs bonded with UV resin, was stiff enough but heavy enough to break the links. A single 3 mm plate was light, but with the ball near the edge it sagged onto the base and the readings became useless. For the third iteration I ran a topology optimization against the ball-at-the-edge load case and compared it in FEA with a conventional pattern of concentric cutouts:
Standard cutouts: 138.0 g, 6.42 mm maximum deflection
The topology-optimized plate was 14% lighter and 12% stiffer, so it went into the build. Every geometry was laser-cut in paper first to check the fit before committing to acrylic.

With the first plate, the links cracked at the joint between link 1 and link 2. As the servos tilted the plate, the heavy ball resisted and pushed a large lateral force down the linkage chain; the link most perpendicular to the tilt took it as shear at the thinnest acrylic around the bearing. I redesigned the links wider around the bearings for shear capacity, added printed end stops so link 2 couldn't peel away from link 1, and rebuilt the joint stack with thin shims, tuning their count by trial until the slop was minimal without binding. It helped, but some play remained: acrylic links on ball joints were the limit, not the tolerances.

The stock MG995 servos stalled outright. 35 kg brushless servos had the torque and almost matched the ping-pong ball's performance, but drew 20 A spikes that no bench supply on campus could deliver. Higher-geared Studica smart servos could lift the load, but on a fast downward tilt the ball drove the plate faster than the servos would follow, back-driving them into generators that tripped the supply. The fix was a protection circuit between the servo shield and the supply: a 15 A Schottky diode to block reverse current, and a 4,700 µF capacitor with a 10 Ω, 100 W dump resistor to absorb and burn off the returned energy.
Getting rid of the ball joints

The slop pointed at a deeper fix, which became our second design question: remove the ball joints altogether. Of six concepts, including cable pulleys, magnetic levitation, two gimbal layouts and slotted links, I took a spherical parallel manipulator forward. It uses pin joints only, with every joint axis passing through one point, so the plate pivots about a fixed centre.

A first concentric-sphere design made aligning the axes and assembling the curved links impractical. The second uses coaxial inputs, base links angled 45° toward the centre axis and three identical L-shaped links, with lengths set so that every axis meets at the same point. Get that slightly wrong and the mechanism either won't assemble or locks to a single degree of freedom. The 3D-printed prototype holds its load at neutral with the motors off, moves smoothly with no bearings at all, and balances an egg.

As a team, we estimate the ball's position from a quasi-static model of the sensor's force and moments, filtered and aligned to the plate, and benchmark it against an OpenCV Hough-circle tracker reworked for the mirror-like steel ball. Control is decoupled X–Y PID with velocity feedforward and extra derivative action to catch the heavy ball's momentum; trajectory planning was compared on a Simulink plant model.
segway: Analyze and model a human transporter, then tune its properties, with no active control, to travel as far as possible before tipping, and compare our Simulink model against an acausal SimulationX model.

We derived the nonlinear kinematic and kinetic equations, linearized them with a small-angle approximation, and swept thrust force and lean angle in Simulink: coarse first, then 160 to 180 N in 0.5 N steps and 0.2 to 0.8 rad in 0.05 rad steps. SimulationX needs no hand-derived equations, so it checked our derivation; Python parsed and plotted its data.

The system is very sensitive to both inputs. Simulink's best was 12.3 m at 170 N and -0.2 rad; SimulationX's was 9.15 m at 110 N and 11°. The gap shows the cost of the idealizations: Simulink suits theoretical analysis, while SimulationX captures more of the physical interactions.
ri3d: As team lead of UW REACT I organized a Robot in 3 Days hackathon: the challenge is unknown until the start, and you build a robot from nothing in 48 hours. With 30% of the turnout I'd planned for, four teammates and I, on about three hours of sleep, built a robot that takes rings and launches them into a goal, with plenty of trips to Canadian Tire and Home Depot despite heavy planning. It served as a reference for the high school teams who then had 6 to 8 weeks to build theirs.
beam-balancer: 1-D ball balancing before the 2-D Stewart platform. I went from choosing the ideal link lengths to 3D modelling the mechanism to final code in about two weeks.
gantry: I wrote STM32 firmware to control a two-axis machine over UART and a potentiometer, with safety stops and homing. Interrupts catch the endstops so the machine never drives past a limit, and I characterized the ADC so the potentiometer sets each axis precisely. The final demo showed safe stops at the limits and a race to position the machine over a target as fast and precisely as possible.
lidar: I wrote a pipeline to manipulate, clean and analyze a massive LiDAR point cloud: removing anomalies, extracting buildings, and finding the two furthest points in a set of millions, a good excuse to try some fun algorithms.
gooseminator: A group project for our mechatronics course: the robot sweeps an area and sorts bird eggs by whether they belong to an invasive or a protected species. The name comes from the running Waterloo joke that the geese are out of control. Our design document covers the full engineering design process.
trashminator: My macro surface-level aquatic cleaning robot. It autonomously navigates a body of water and collects floating trash, and a swarm of them could help fight aquatic pollution. It started as a technological design course project and became a personal one I kept improving.
robotic-arm: A 3-degree-of-freedom arm built in under 8 hours from a Tetrix kit for rapid prototyping. It picks up oddly shaped bones and places them in containers at different locations.
